pages.p: An **operator** is a symbol that does something with values. The maths ones are «+», «-», «*» (times) and «/» (divide). JavaScript follows normal maths order: «*» and «/» come before «+» and «-». Brackets go first.
pages.tip: There is only one number type, so «10 / 4» is simply 2.5. No special rule for whole numbers.

pages.p:
The «%» operator gives the **remainder** after a division. Think of sharing sweets: 10 sweets for 3 friends is 3 each, and 1 is left over.

A classic use: a number is even when «n % 2» is 0.
Two stars mean "to the power of". «2 ** 3» is 2 times 2 times 2. Powers are worked out before «*» and «/».
Updating a variable is so common that JavaScript has shortcuts. «n += 5» means «n = n + 5». The same works for «-=», «*=» and «/=». For adding or taking away exactly 1, use «++» and «--».
pages.tip: These only work on variables made with «let», because the value changes.

pages.p:
A comparison asks a question and the answer is a boolean. Use «===» for "is equal to", «!==» for "is not equal to", and «<», «>», «<=», «>=».

Remember: one «=» stores a value. Three «===» compare.
«===» is strict: the types must match too. The number 5 and the text «"5"» look alike, but they are different types, so they are not equal. Always use «===», not the older «==».
pages.tip: Capital letters matter too: «"a"» is not «"A"».

pages.p:
Join booleans with logical operators:

• «&&» (and): true only if **both** sides are true
• «||» (or): true if **at least one** side is true
• «!» (not): flips true to false and false to true

Put a comparison on each side of «&&» or «||» to ask a bigger question. Comparisons are worked out first.

Here we check if a number is between 1 and 10.
pages.tip: Write «n >= 1 && n <= 10». Writing «1 <= n <= 10» does not work the way you expect.

pages.p:
JavaScript has a ready-made toolbox called «Math».

• «Math.round(x)»: nearest whole number
• «Math.floor(x)»: round **down**
• «Math.ceil(x)»: round **up**
• «Math.max(a, b, ...)» and «Math.min(a, b, ...)»: the biggest and smallest
«floor» goes toward the **smaller** number and «ceil» toward the **bigger** number. For positive numbers that looks like "cut the decimals" and "round up", but with negatives it is different.
pages.tip: Need whole boxes to fit 10 items, 3 per box? «Math.ceil(10 / 3)» gives 4.

pages.p: With two numbers, «+» adds. If one side is a string, «+» joins, and the number turns into text. JavaScript reads from left to right. The other operators «-», «*» and «/» always do maths, and turn text that looks like a number into a number.

When a maths operation makes no sense, you get «NaN», which means "Not a Number". It appears if you convert text that is not a number. Odd but true: «NaN» is a number type, and it is not equal to itself.
pages.tip: Seeing NaN in your output? A value that you expected to be a number is not one.

hand.why: Multiplication comes first: 3 * 2 = 6, then 7 + 6 = 13. Brackets would be needed to get 20.
10 divided by 3 is 3 with 1 left over. «%» gives that remainder.
«2 ** 3» means 2 * 2 * 2, which is 8. It is not 2 * 3.
One side is a string, so «+» joins the pieces: the text «34».

hand.q: Complete the line so total becomes 14.
hand.why: «total += 4» is the short form of «total = total + 4».
«===» also compares types. A number and a string are never strictly equal.
Each comparison gives its own boolean. «8 > 3» is true, and «8 < 3» is false.

hand.q: Which operator means "is not equal to"?
hand.why: «!==» is the strict "not equal". It is the opposite of «===».
«&&» needs both sides to be true. One false side makes everything false.
«3 > 5» is false, and «!» flips it to true.
«round» goes to the nearest (5), «floor» goes down (4), and «ceil» always goes up, so 4.2 becomes 5.
«Math.max» returns the biggest of the values you give it.

hand.q: Put the lines in order so that 2 is printed.
hand.why: The variable is created first. «lives--» takes one away, and then the new value is printed.

hand.q: Complete the test for an even number.
hand.why: A number is even when dividing by 2 leaves remainder 0. The «%» operator gives the remainder.

hard.why: First x becomes 10 - 3 = 7, then 7 * 2 = 14. Each step uses the latest value.
«-» does maths and turns «"10"» into a number: 6. «+» joins text: «104».
17 = 3 * 5 + 2, so the remainder is 2. And 17 % 2 is 1, so the comparison is true.
«floor» goes toward the smaller number, -2. «ceil» goes toward the bigger one, -1.
NaN has the type number, but it is never equal to anything, not even itself.
7 is bigger than 5 (true), but 7 % 2 is 1, not 0 (false). «&&» needs both to be true.

hard.q: Which test is true when age is from 13 to 19, including both ends?
hard.why: Both conditions must hold, so we need «&&». With «||» every number passes, and «>» or «<» would leave out 13 and 19.

hard.q: Boxes hold 10 items. How many boxes do 25 items need?
hard.why: 25 / 10 = 2.5, but you cannot buy half a box. «Math.ceil» rounds up to 3.
JavaScript reads left to right. «"Total: " + 2» becomes text, and then 3 is joined to that text.

items.symptom: It prints 7, but true was expected.
items.why: One «=» stores a value. To compare, use three: «===».

items.symptom: The average of 4 and 8 should be 6, but it prints 8.
items.why: Division happens before addition. Brackets make the sum happen first.

items.symptom: It prints false, but 8 is an even number.
items.why: Even means the remainder is 0, so use «%». «n / 2» is 4.
«=-» stores minus one. The shortcut for subtracting is «-=», in that order.

items.symptom: It prints 2 pages, but 21 items need 3 pages.
items.why: «round» turns 2.1 into 2. «ceil» always rounds up, so no item is left out.

items.symptom: It prints true, but the shop is closed at 3.
items.why: With «||» one true side is enough, and every hour passes one of them. Use «&&» so both must hold.

project.title: Bill Splitter
project.brief:
Write a function «splitBill» with three inputs: «total» (the bill), «people» (how many share it) and «tipPercent» (the tip, like 10 for 10%).

Add the tip to the bill, divide by the number of people, and **round up** to a whole number, so nobody pays too little. Return that number.

Example: «splitBill(100, 3, 15)» returns «39» (115 split 3 ways is 38.33, rounded up).
